questions.stem: Inspiration occurs as a result of:

options.label: A
options.text: an upward movement of the diaphragm

options.label: B
options.text: upward and outward movement of the ribs due to contraction of the external intercostal muscles

questions.why: Inspiration is an active process driven by the downward contraction of the diaphragm and the outward/upward movement of the ribs (external intercostals).

notes.A: The diaphragm moves DOWN in inspiration.

questions.stem: In order for the lungs to function normally, the intrapleural pressure must:

options.label: B
options.text: be between +5 and +10 mmHg above the atmospheric pressure

options.label: C
options.text: alternate between being less than and greater than the atmospheric pressure

options.label: D
options.text: change as respiratory demands of the body change

options.label: E
options.text: be the same as the atmospheric pressure

questions.why: A negative (subatmospheric) intrapleural pressure relative to alveolar pressure is essential to keep the lungs expanded.

notes.C: It stays subatmospheric in quiet breathing.
notes.D: It does vary, but staying below alveolar pressure is what keeps the lungs open.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the site of the highest airway resistance?
questions.why: While the total cross-sectional area is smaller higher up, the medium-sized bronchi contribute the most to total airway resistance.

notes.A: The mouth contributes little at rest.
notes.B: The largest bronchi carry less resistance than medium ones.
notes.D: Small airways are numerous, in parallel, so their total resistance is low.

questions.stem: Vital Capacity includes:
questions.why: Vital Capacity = Tidal Volume + Inspiratory Reserve Volume + Expiratory Reserve Volume. It excludes Residual Volume.

notes.A: Included, along with ERV and IRV.
notes.B: Included, along with TV and IRV.
notes.C: RV is NOT part of VC.
notes.D: Included, along with TV and ERV.

questions.stem: Which muscles contract in quiet breathing?
questions.why: Quiet inspiration is driven primarily by the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles.

notes.B: Correct, but the diaphragm also contracts.
notes.C: Correct, but the external intercostals also contract.

questions.stem: Surfactant:

options.label: A
options.text: is produced by type I alveolar cells

options.label: D
options.text: reduces blood flow to the lungs

questions.why: Surfactant reduces surface tension, which prevents alveolar collapse and significantly increases pulmonary compliance.

notes.D: It does not affect blood flow.

questions.stem: Obligatory respiratory muscles are:

options.label: A
options.text: the diaphragm and mm. intercostales interni

options.label: B
options.text: the diaphragm and mm. intercostales externi

questions.why: The diaphragm and external intercostals are the primary (obligatory) muscles of quiet inspiration.

questions.stem: For the surfactant it is true that:

options.label: A
options.text: is produced by type II alveolar cells

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: decreases the alveolar surface tension at the end of expiration

options.label: D

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.D: True, but so are the other statements.

questions.stem: Normal breathing at rest is called:
questions.why: Eupnea is the medical term for normal, quiet breathing at rest.

questions.stem: During expiration:

options.label: A
options.text: the thoracic cage recoils and the diaphragm moves upwards

questions.why: Expiration is typically passive: the diaphragm relaxes (moves up) and the chest wall recoils. This increases (makes less negative) intrapleural pressure.

notes.A: True, but C is also true.
notes.C: True, but A is also true.

questions.stem: Tidal Volume (TV) is:

options.label: A
options.text: the volume of air, which passes through the lungs per minute

options.label: C
options.text: an element of the Functional Residual Capacity (FRC)

questions.why: Normal tidal volume is about 500 mL (0.5 L).

notes.B: RV (about 1.2 L) is bigger than TV.
notes.D: A, B and C are false.

questions.stem: The intrapleural pressure is:

options.label: D
options.text: depends on the water molecules' surface tension and elastic fibers

questions.why: Intrapleural pressure is subatmospheric (about −4 mmHg at rest) because the lung's elastic fibres and alveolar surface tension pull the lung inward while the chest wall pulls outward.

notes.B: True, but D is also true.
notes.D: True, but B is also true.

questions.stem: The anatomical dead space:

options.label: A
options.text: includes the volume of air in the alveoli

options.label: B
options.text: is the space where most gas exchange occurs

questions.why: Anatomical dead space (the conducting airways) is normally about 150 mL (the exam key says 140 mL, which is acceptable).

notes.E: That is a minute ventilation figure.

questions.stem: The Residual Volume (RV) is:

options.label: A
options.text: the volume of air, which remains in the lungs after maximal expiration

options.label: B
options.text: the volume of air, which remains in the lungs after maximal inspiration

options.label: D
options.text: is the tidal volume plus the inspiratory reserve volume

options.label: E
options.text: a component of the Vital Capacity (VC)

questions.why: RV is the air left in the lungs after a maximal forced expiration. It is not part of vital capacity.

notes.E: RV is not part of VC.

questions.stem: It is not true that Vital Capacity (VC):
questions.why: VC does NOT include residual volume (RV). VC = TV + IRV + ERV.

notes.B: True: VC varies with sex and age.
notes.C: True: VC varies with body size.

questions.stem: There are smooth muscles in the respiratory system:

options.label: A
options.text: on the external surface of the lungs

options.label: B
options.text: on the medial surface of the lungs

options.label: C
options.text: in the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles

options.label: E
options.text: on the external and medial surfaces of the lungs

questions.why: Smooth muscle is found in the walls of the airways (trachea, bronchi, bronchioles), controlling their diameter. Alveoli lack smooth muscle.

notes.A: The lung surface (pleura) has no smooth muscle layer.
notes.B: The lung surface (pleura) has no smooth muscle layer.
notes.E: The lung surfaces (pleura) have no smooth muscle layer.

questions.stem: The elastic fibers in the lungs are situated:

options.label: B
options.text: around the terminal branches of the bronchi

options.label: C
options.text: on the external and the medial surface of the lungs

questions.why: Elastic fibers are distributed throughout the lung parenchyma (alveoli, airways, and pleural surfaces) to provide elastic recoil.

notes.A: True, but they are elsewhere too.
notes.B: True, but they are elsewhere too.
notes.C: True, but they are elsewhere too.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not happen during inspiration?

options.label: C
options.text: the antero-posterior dimensions of the chest are increased

options.label: D
options.text: the transverse dimensions of the thorax are increased

options.label: E
options.text: the scalene and sternocleidomastoid muscles can be recruited for inspiration

questions.why: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and moves DOWNWARD, not upward.

questions.stem: Total Lung Capacity (TLC) of men would normally be about:
questions.why: Normal TLC is approximately 6 liters (6000 mL) in an average adult male.

notes.A: 4200 ml is about the vital capacity.

questions.stem: The surfactant:

options.label: B
options.text: reduces the surface tension of the water layer within alveoli

options.label: D
options.text: increases in concentration when the sympathetic tone is increased

questions.why: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse at the end of expiration.

notes.A: It makes the lungs EASIER to inflate and keeps them stable in expiration.
notes.C: It does not act on smooth muscle.

questions.stem: Pulmonary surfactant increases:

options.label: A
options.text: the surface tension of the fluid lining alveolar walls

options.label: C
options.text: in effectiveness as the lungs are inflated

options.label: D
options.text: in amount when pulmonary blood flow is interrupted

questions.why: Surfactant lowers surface tension, which increases pulmonary compliance (making the lungs easier to inflate).

notes.C: It works BEST when alveoli are small.
notes.E: It does not act on bronchi.

questions.stem: During inspiration:

options.label: A
options.text: intrapleural pressure is lowest at midinspiration

options.label: B
options.text: intrapulmonary pressure is lowest around mid-inspiration

options.label: C
options.text: intraoesophageal pressure is lowest at midinspiration

options.label: D
options.text: the rate of air flow is greatest at endinspiration

options.label: E
options.text: the lung volume/intrapleural pressure relationship is the same as in expiration

questions.why: Intrapulmonary (alveolar) pressure drops below atmospheric pressure during inspiration, reaching its lowest point mid-inspiration when airflow is highest.

notes.A: Intrapleural pressure is lowest at END inspiration.
notes.C: Oesophageal pressure follows pleural pressure (lowest at end).
notes.D: Flow is greatest at MID inspiration.

questions.stem: During inspiration:

options.label: A
options.text: venous return to the heart is increased

options.label: B
options.text: less energy is expended than during expiration

options.label: C
options.text: lung expansion is assisted by surface tension forces in the alveoli

options.label: D
options.text: lung expansion begins when intrapleural pressure falls below atmospheric

options.label: E
options.text: the relative concentration of surfactant increases in alveoli

questions.why: The decrease in intrathoracic pressure during inspiration draws more blood into the thoracic veins, increasing venous return.

notes.E: Surfactant is diluted as alveoli expand.

questions.stem: The residual volume (RV) is:

options.label: A
options.text: the volume of air remaining in the lungs at the end of a maximal expiration

options.label: B
options.text: greater on average in women than in men

options.label: C
options.text: 3-4 litres on average in young adults

options.label: E
options.text: smaller in old than in young people

questions.why: RV is the air left in the lungs after the most forceful expiration. It cannot be measured directly by a spirometer.

notes.B: It is greater in men (larger lungs).
notes.E: RV is LARGER in the elderly.

questions.stem: The compliance of the lungs and chest wall is:

options.label: A
options.text: expressed as volume change per unit change in pressure

options.label: C
options.text: increased by the surface tension of the fluid lining the alveoli

options.label: E
options.text: changed by parallel displacement of the line relating lung volume to distending pressure

questions.why: Compliance is defined as the change in lung volume per unit change in transpulmonary pressure (ΔV/ΔP).

notes.E: Compliance is the slope; a parallel shift keeps it.

questions.stem: Respiratory dead space:

options.label: A
options.text: includes the volume of air in the airways up to the terminal bronchi

options.label: B
options.text: is where the gas exchange occur

options.label: D
options.text: makes great changes in O2 and CO2 contain in alveolar air

options.label: E
options.text: includes the volume of air which reaches the alveoli

questions.why: Anatomical dead space is the volume of the conducting airways where no gas exchange occurs.

notes.D: It has little effect at normal tidal volumes.
notes.E: Air that reaches the alveoli is alveolar ventilation.

questions.stem: Air in the pleural cavity (pneumothorax):

options.label: A
options.text: allows intrapleural pressure to rise and become equal to the atmospheric pressure

options.label: B
options.text: causes the underlying lung to collapse by compressing it

options.label: D
options.text: leads to a slight inward movement of the chest wall

questions.why: In pneumothorax, the negative intrapleural pressure is lost, causing the lung to collapse.

notes.B: The lung collapses by its own recoil.

questions.stem: Loss of pulmonary elastic tissue in 'emphysema' reduces:
questions.why: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and elastic recoil, leading to air trapping (increased RV) and decreased vital capacity.

questions.stem: Complete obstruction of a major bronchus usually results in:

options.label: A
options.text: collapse of the alveoli supplied by the bronchus

options.label: B
options.text: a rise in local intrapleural pressure

options.label: C
options.text: an increase in physiological dead space

options.label: D
options.text: an increase in blood flow to the lung tissue supplied by the bronchus

questions.why: Air trapped behind a complete obstruction is absorbed, causing the alveoli to collapse (atelectasis).

notes.E: Not usual with one major bronchus.

questions.stem: For air to enter the lungs during inspiration:

options.label: A
options.text: the pressure inside the lungs must be higher than the atmospheric pressure

options.label: B
options.text: the pressure inside the lungs must become lower than the atmospheric pressure

options.label: C
options.text: the pressure inside the lungs must be equal to the atmospheric pressure

options.label: E
options.text: the external intercostal muscles must be relaxed

questions.why: Air flows into the lungs due to a pressure gradient. Intra-alveolar pressure must drop below atmospheric pressure.

questions.stem: If forcefully exhaling as much air as possible after a normal breath, this is:
questions.why: The extra volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal expiration is the expiratory reserve volume (ERV).

notes.C: That is a flow, not a volume.

questions.stem: Water molecules on the surface of the alveoli generate surface tension. This force:
questions.why: Surface tension acts to minimize surface area, assisting in elastic recoil (which helps expiration). Surfactant reduces this tension.

notes.E: Its main effect is on recoil and compliance.

questions.stem: The normal FEV1/FVC ratio in an adult is about:
questions.why: Normal FEV1/FVC ratio is approximately 80%.

questions.stem: Intrapleural pressure:

options.label: A
options.text: is higher than the atmospheric one as in inspiration

options.label: B
options.text: is lower than the atmospheric one as in inspiration

options.label: D
options.text: does not depend on the water molecules

options.label: E
options.text: does not change when pleural cavity hermeticity is impaired

questions.why: Intrapleural pressure is normally subatmospheric (negative), and becomes even more negative during inspiration.

notes.A: It is never above atmospheric in quiet breathing.

questions.stem: Surfactant is secreted by:
questions.why: Type II alveolar cells secrete pulmonary surfactant.

notes.B: Type I cells are for exchange.
notes.E: Smooth muscle does not secrete it.

questions.stem: Airway resistance:

options.label: D
options.text: does not affect work of breathing

questions.why: Asthma causes bronchoconstriction and increased mucus, significantly increasing airway resistance.

questions.stem: The intrapleural pressure at the end of quiet expiration is about:
questions.why: At FRC the inward recoil of the lung and the outward recoil of the chest wall give an intrapleural pressure of about −5 cmH2O (−4 mmHg). It falls to about −6 mmHg at the end of quiet inspiration and much lower in deep inspiration.

notes.B: It is never positive in quiet breathing.
notes.C: That is end of quiet INSPIRATION.

questions.stem: The pulmonary ventilation is a process that includes:

options.label: D
options.text: exchange of O2 and CO2 via the capillary walls

options.label: E
options.text: transport of O2 and CO2 via blood

questions.why: Pulmonary ventilation is the mechanical process of moving air in (inspiration) and out (expiration) of the lungs.

questions.stem: During inspiration:

options.label: A
options.text: the water surface tension in alveoli decreases

options.label: B
options.text: the chest volume decreases and the diaphragm goes up

questions.why: During inspiration, the expansion of the thoracic cavity causes intrapleural pressure to become more negative (decreases).

notes.A: Surface tension RISES as alveoli expand.
notes.B: The chest ENLARGES and the diaphragm goes DOWN.

questions.stem: Which of the following events are sympathetic effects?
questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation causes bronchodilation (via beta-2) and pulmonary vasoconstriction (via alpha-1).

questions.stem: The bronchial muscles relax under the influence of:
questions.why: Epinephrine (beta-2 agonist) causes bronchodilation, and atropine (muscarinic antagonist) blocks cholinergic bronchoconstriction.

notes.A: True, but atropine also relaxes them.
notes.B: True, but adrenaline also relaxes them.

questions.stem: Dilation of bronchi can be achieved by:

options.label: C
options.text: increase of acetylcholine and serotonin levels

options.label: D
options.text: increase of bradikinine and histamine levels

questions.why: Catecholamines (like epinephrine) stimulate beta-2 receptors to cause bronchodilation.

questions.stem: The sympathetic division of ANS affects the bronchial muscles activating:
questions.why: Sympathetic innervation causes bronchodilation via beta-2 adrenergic receptors.

notes.A: Alpha receptors play little part in bronchial muscle.
notes.E: H2 receptors are not the sympathetic route.

questions.stem: The bronchodilatory effect of atropin is due to blocking:
questions.why: Atropine blocks muscarinic (M) cholinergic receptors, preventing parasympathetically mediated bronchoconstriction.

notes.A: Atropine does not block N receptors.
notes.C: Atropine is not an α blocker.

questions.stem: The bronchial muscles relax under the influence of:
questions.why: Atropine blocks cholinergic constriction, causing bronchodilation (relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle).

questions.stem: Bronchial smooth muscle contracts in response to:
questions.why: Irritation triggers parasympathetic reflexes that cause bronchoconstriction to protect the airways.

questions.stem: Bronchial asthma is likely to be relieved by:
questions.why: Beta-adrenergic agonists (like albuterol) cause bronchodilation and are mainstays of asthma treatment.

questions.stem: Histamine affects the bronchial muscles via:
questions.why: Histamine binds to H1 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, causing bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: Coughing:

options.label: A
options.text: is reflexly initiated by irritation of the alveoli

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: depends on contraction of the diaphragm for expulsion of air

options.label: D
options.text: differs from sneezing in that the glottis is initially closed

questions.stem: The sympathetic branch of the Autonomic Nervous System affects the bronchial muscles via:
questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation of β2-adrenergic receptors causes bronchodilation.

notes.B: α2 is not the bronchial route.

questions.stem: The bronchial muscles increase their tone under the influence of:
questions.why: Histamine is a potent bronchoconstrictor (increases tone) involved in allergic asthma.

questions.stem: The bronchial muscles dilate under the influence of:
questions.why: Catecholamines (like epinephrine) act on beta-2 receptors to dilate the bronchial muscles.

questions.stem: Most of the CO2 that is transported in blood is:
questions.why: About 70% of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) in the plasma, generated by carbonic anhydrase in RBCs.

notes.C: Carbonic acid is transient and very small.
notes.E: This is an enzyme, not a carrier.

questions.stem: In which vascular bed does hypoxia cause vasoconstriction?
questions.why: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is a unique mechanism in the lungs to divert blood away from poorly ventilated areas to optimize gas exchange.

notes.E: Skin vessels are under neural control.

questions.stem: Compared with the systemic circulation, the pulmonary circulation has a:
questions.why: Pulmonary circulation is a high-flow, low-resistance, low-pressure system.

notes.A: Flow is the SAME (the whole cardiac output).
notes.C: Pulmonary pressure is about 15 mmHg vs 95.
notes.E: Output is the same in both.

questions.stem: Hypoventilation will cause:
questions.why: Hypoventilation leads to increased CO2 (hypercapnia) and decreased O2 (hypoxia) in the blood.

questions.stem: Which of the following events is caused by an increased pCO2 in tissues?

options.label: B
options.text: decreased association between hemoglobin and O2

questions.why: Increased pCO2 decreases pH (acidosis) and shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right (Bohr effect), decreasing O2 affinity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is related to the respiratory function of the lungs?

options.label: C
options.text: diffusion of gases between the alveolar air and blood

questions.why: Ventilation and gas diffusion are the primary respiratory functions of the lungs.

questions.stem: Which factors affect the gas diffusion through the respiratory membrane?
questions.why: Fick's law states diffusion is proportional to area and inversely proportional to thickness, alongside partial pressure gradients.

notes.C: Tidal volume affects ventilation, not membrane diffusion.
notes.D: RV does not affect diffusion across the membrane.

questions.stem: Gas exchange in the respiratory system of humans takes place in the:
questions.why: Alveoli are the primary sites of gas exchange in the lungs.

notes.C: Mostly conducting; only respiratory bronchioles exchange a little.

questions.stem: As regards the distribution of ventilation (V) and perfusion (Q), the V/Q ratio:

options.label: A
options.text: gradient of change of ventilation is greater than that of perfusion

options.label: D
options.text: at apex is greater than at base in prone position

notes.D: In the prone position the gradient is largely lost.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide transport is:
questions.why: Approximately 70% of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate in the plasma.

questions.stem: For the alveolar capillary membrane it is true that:

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: has better permeability for O2 than CO2

questions.why: The respiratory membrane consists of the alveolar and capillary walls. CO2 is actually more soluble and diffuses faster than O2, so statement 'c' is false.

notes.A: True, but B is also true.
notes.B: True, but A is also true.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors shifts the dissociation curve of HbO2 to the right:
questions.why: Increased pCO2 lowers pH (Bohr effect) and shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, facilitating oxygen unloading.

notes.D: pO2 itself does not shift the curve.

questions.stem: It is true that the air in the alveoli:

options.label: A
options.text: has a higher CO2 content than the atmosphere

options.label: B
options.text: has lower O2 content than in the atmosphere

options.label: C
options.text: consists of N2 approximately equal to that in the atmosphere

options.label: D
options.text: has the same components as the atmosphere

notes.A: True, but B and C are also true.
notes.B: True, but A and C are also true.
notes.C: True, but A and B are also true.

options.text: carbamino Hb and physically dissolved in the fluids

questions.stem: The ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio of 0.8 refers to:

options.text: the middle parts of the lungs in upright position

options.text: the lower parts of the lungs in upright position

questions.stem: Oxygen enters the cell via?
questions.why: Oxygen moves from areas of higher partial pressure to lower partial pressure via simple diffusion.

questions.stem: Most of the carbon dioxide produced by tissues is transported to the lungs as:

options.label: A

questions.why: Gas exchange occurs across the alveolar-capillary membrane in the pulmonary capillaries.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin gives up oxygen when the environment is more:
questions.why: The Bohr effect states that a lower pH (more acidic) shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, facilitating oxygen unloading.

notes.B: Alkaline conditions hold O2 more tightly.

questions.stem: In the lungs:

options.label: A
options.text: the rate of alveolar ventilation at rest exceeds the rate of alveolar capillary perfusion

options.label: B
options.text: the ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio in less 0.6 during maximal exercise

questions.stem: Pulmonary:

options.label: A

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide is carried in the blood in:

questions.stem: The correct statement is:

options.label: A
options.text: the diffusion velocity of O2 and CO2 is equal

options.label: B
options.text: O2 diffuses 20 times faster than CO2

options.text: CO2 diffuses about 20 times faster than O2

options.label: B
options.text: blood saturates with CO2 when pCO2 exceeds normal alveolar levels

questions.why: The Haldane effect states that oxygenation of hemoglobin in the lungs reduces its affinity for CO2, driving CO2 out of the blood.

notes.A: The CO2 curve is nearly linear.
notes.C: With zero pCO2 there is no CO2.
notes.E: That is the Bohr effect, seen on the O2 curve.

questions.stem: A shift of the oxygen dissociation curve of blood to the left:

options.label: A
options.text: decreases the O2 content of blood at a given pO2

options.label: B
options.text: impairs O2 delivery to the tissues at the normal tissue pO2

options.label: C
options.text: occurs in blood perfusing hot extremities

options.label: D
options.text: occurs in blood with lower pH than with higher pH

options.label: E
options.text: is characteristic of adult blood when compared with fetal blood

questions.why: A leftward shift increases O2 affinity, making it harder for hemoglobin to release O2 to the tissues.

notes.A: Content at a given pO2 INCREASES.

questions.stem: Cyanosis:

options.label: A
options.text: may be caused by high levels of carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood

options.label: B
options.text: may be caused by high levels of methaemoglobin in the blood

options.label: C
options.text: is seen in fingers of hands immersed in iced water

options.label: D
options.text: occurs more easily in anaemic than in polycythaemic patients

questions.why: Methemoglobinemia (e.g., from nitrites) causes cyanosis because the oxidized iron cannot bind oxygen.

notes.C: Cold blood holds O2 and the skin is red.
notes.E: In cyanide poisoning venous blood stays oxygenated.

questions.stem: A 50 % fall in the ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio in each of lungs would:

options.label: B
options.text: has no effect on the O2 in systemic circulation

options.label: D
options.text: lower systemic arterial carbon dioxide content

options.label: E
options.text: be compensated (with respect to oxygen uptake) by a high ratio in the other lung

questions.why: A significant drop in V/Q ratio means shunting (perfusion without adequate ventilation), which lowers systemic arterial O2.

notes.C: Low V/Q acts as a shunt, not dead space.
notes.D: CO2 tends to rise or stay the same.
notes.E: High V/Q cannot add O2 to saturated blood.

questions.stem: The total amount of O2 carried by the circulation to the tissues/min. (oxygen delivery or total available oxygen):

options.label: A
options.text: normally equals the rate of O2 consumption by the body/min

options.label: B
options.text: is normally more than 95 per cent combined with haemoglobin

options.label: C
options.text: must fall by about half if haemoglobin concentration is halved

options.label: D
options.text: is more closely related to PO2 than to percentage saturation of the blood with O2

options.label: E
options.text: must double if body oxygen consumption doubles

questions.why: Almost all oxygen (97-98%) is transported bound to hemoglobin.

notes.C: Not necessarily, since cardiac output can compensate.

questions.stem: Given: CO2 + H2O -> H2CO3-> HCO3- + H+, what happens if bicarbonate ions are increased?

options.label: D
options.text: there would be a shift to the left

options.label: E
options.text: there would be a shift to the right first, then to the left

questions.why: By Le Chatelier's principle, increasing the product (HCO3-) drives the reaction to the left, forming more CO2 and H2O.

questions.stem: The values (mm Hg) for pCO2 and pO2 in the interstitial spaces of peripheral tissues are approximately:
questions.why: In peripheral tissues, cells consume O2 (dropping pO2 to ~40 mmHg) and produce CO2 (raising pCO2 to ~46 mmHg).

questions.stem: Which of the following reactions takes place in the systemic capillaries (where CO2 is increased and O2 is decreased)?
questions.why: In systemic tissues, CO2 binds to hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin (HbCO2).

questions.stem: Which of the following factors decrease the affinity of Hb to O2 in tissues:

options.label: E
options.text: decreased pCO2, higher pH and lowered to

questions.why: The Bohr effect: increased pCO2 and lowered pH shift the dissociation curve to the right, decreasing Hb's affinity for O2.

questions.stem: The exchange of O2 and CO2 between the capillary blood and the cells is carried out by:
questions.why: Gas exchange between blood and tissues occurs via simple diffusion down partial pressure gradients.

questions.stem: The peripheral chemoreceptors are situated:

options.label: A
options.text: on the ventral surface of medulla oblongata

options.label: B
options.text: on the dorsal surface of medulla oblongata

options.label: C
options.text: in arcus aortae and arteria carotis communis

options.label: D
options.text: in the inferior and superior venae cavae and the right atrium

questions.why: Peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies (carotid bifurcation) and aortic bodies (aortic arch).

notes.E: The hypothalamus is not chemoreceptive for breathing.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors increases the rate of breathing:
questions.why: High CO2 (hypercapnia) and low O2 (hypoxia) are potent stimulators of the respiratory centers.

questions.stem: The need to breathe is caused by:

options.label: C
options.text: a drop in blood oxygen levels

options.label: D
options.text: a drop in carbon dioxide levels

questions.why: The primary drive to breathe is an increase in CO2 (hypercapnia), which lowers blood pH (increases H+ concentration).

notes.C: Hypoxia stimulates only when severe; CO2/H+ is the main drive.

questions.stem: Acidosis is when blood pH is below?
questions.why: Normal blood pH is 7.35 - 7.45. Acidosis is a pH below 7.35.

notes.C: That is acidosis, but the cut-off is 7.35.

questions.stem: The carotid bodies:

options.label: A
options.text: are stretch receptors in the walls of the internal carotid arteries

options.label: B
options.text: have a blood flow per unit volume similar to that in the brain

options.label: C
options.text: are inhibited by a rise in blood pCO2

options.label: D
options.text: generate fewer afferent impulses when blood H+ concentration rises

options.label: E
options.text: and the aortic bodies are mainly responsible for the increased ventilation in hypoxia

questions.why: Carotid and aortic bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors primarily responsible for detecting hypoxia and stimulating ventilation.

notes.A: They are chemoreceptors at the bifurcation.
notes.B: Their flow is far higher (about 2 L/100 g/min).

questions.stem: The hemoreceptors in the carotid artery and aortic arc are excited when:
questions.why: Peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated primarily by a decrease in arterial pO2 (hypoxia).

questions.stem: Which of the following factors stimulate respiration:
questions.why: High CO2 and low O2 strongly stimulate respiration. (Note: Alkalosis typically inhibits respiration, but based on the options, E contains the correct stimulating factors).

questions.stem: A rise in arterial pCO2 causes:

options.label: A
options.text: an increase in ventilation due to stimulation of peripheral and central chemoreceptors

options.label: B
options.text: a decrease in ventilation due to stimulation of central and peripheral chemoreceptors

options.label: D
options.text: a decrease in cerebral blood flow

options.label: E
options.text: a decrease in the plasma bicarbonate level

questions.why: Hypercapnia stimulates both central (medullary) and peripheral chemoreceptors to increase ventilation.

questions.stem: Ventilation is increased during:

options.label: A
options.text: periods when cerebrospinal fluid pH is reduced

options.label: C
options.text: periods when plasma bicarbonate level is increased

options.label: E
options.text: exercise because of the ensuing fall in arterial pO2

questions.why: A decrease in CSF pH (due to increased CO2) strongly stimulates the central respiratory centers.

notes.E: Arterial pO2 does not fall in moderate exercise.

questions.stem: What does the ventral respiratory group within the medulla oblongata do?

options.label: E
options.text: inhibits apneustic center, sets limit to over inflation of lungs

questions.why: The VRG is primarily active during forceful expiration and forced breathing, whereas the DRG handles quiet inspiration.

notes.C: It is active in forced breathing.

questions.stem: The region in the brain that sets the limit for over-inflation of lungs is located in the:
questions.why: The pneumotaxic center in the pons inhibits the apneustic center, limiting inspiration and preventing over-inflation.

notes.D: The pons, not the medulla, contains the pneumotaxic centre.

questions.stem: The most important gas maintaining alveolar ventilation is:
questions.why: CO2 is the primary regulator of respiration, acting on central chemoreceptors.

notes.A: O2 drives breathing only when it falls a lot.

questions.stem: Decrease of pCO2, decrease in H+ and increased pO2 causes:
questions.why: Low CO2 (hypocapnia) and high O2 remove the stimulus for breathing, causing hypoventilation.

notes.A: These REDUCE the drive to breathe.

questions.stem: Sudden complete obstruction of the respiratory tract causes:
questions.why: Complete obstruction prevents ventilation, causing CO2 retention, which directly stimulates central chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: Oxygen debt is:

options.label: A
options.text: the total amount of O2 consumed during exercise

options.label: B
options.text: incurred because the pulmonary capillary walls limit O2 uptake during exercise

options.label: C
options.text: possible since skeletal muscle can function temporarily without oxygen

options.label: D
options.text: associated with a decrease in blood lactate

questions.why: Oxygen debt occurs because muscles can perform anaerobic metabolism temporarily, creating an oxygen deficit that must be repaid later.

notes.A: The debt is the EXTRA O2 consumed after exercise.
notes.E: It is linked to lactic ACIDOSIS.

questions.stem: A diver breathing air at a depth of 30 metres under water:

options.label: A
options.text: is exposed to a pressure equal to that at the surface

options.label: B
options.text: has a raised pressure of nitrogen in the alveoli

options.label: C
options.text: has a four-fold increase in the oxygen content of blood

options.label: D
options.text: has a four-fold increase in alveolar water vapour pressure

options.label: E
options.text: Expends less energy than normal on the work of breathing

questions.why: At 30m depth, total pressure is 4 atmospheres. The partial pressure of nitrogen rises significantly, increasing the risk of nitrogen narcosis and decompression sickness.

notes.C: Hb is already saturated; dissolved O2 rises only a little.
notes.D: Water vapour pressure depends only on temperature.
notes.E: Dense gas INCREASES the work of breathing.

questions.stem: In Caissons disease pain in the joints and muscles is due to:

options.label: D
options.text: due to increase in barometric pressure

questions.why: Decompression sickness (Caissons disease) occurs when nitrogen bubbles form in the blood and tissues due to rapid pressure reduction.

notes.C: The pain is not due to fatigue.
notes.E: O2 is used up by tissues.

questions.stem: As one ascends to higher than 3000 meters above sea level changes in alveolar pO2 and pCO2 are as follows:

options.label: A
options.text: decrease in pO2, increase in pCO2

options.label: B
options.text: decrease in pO2, decrease in pCO2

options.label: C
options.text: increase in both pO2 and pCO2

options.label: D
options.text: increase in pO2, decrease in pCO2

options.label: E
options.text: no change in pO2 and pCO2

questions.why: At high altitude, lower atmospheric pressure reduces pO2. Hyperventilation (triggered by hypoxia) blows off more CO2, decreasing pCO2.

questions.stem: Which of the following effects is not observed during prolonged stay is space:
questions.why: In microgravity, astronauts experience a decrease in red cell mass (space anemia), not an increase.

questions.stem: Exercise which doubles the metabolic rate is likely to at least double the:
questions.why: Oxygen consumption (VO2) increases linearly with metabolic rate during exercise.

notes.B: Cardiac output rises less than oxygen consumption.

questions.stem: The effects of moving from sea level to an altitude of 5000 metres include an increase in:
questions.why: Hypoxia at high altitude stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors, significantly increasing alveolar ventilation.
